title: What Is a Fluid?
lead: A fluid is a state of matter that yields to a sideways, or shearing, force, and liquids, gases, and plasmas all do. This section names the common phases of matter, says which of them keep a shape and which keep a volume, and explains the difference by the forces between the atoms: held near fixed places in a solid, in contact but free to slide past one another in a liquid, and far apart and free to move in a gas or a plasma.
objectives: State the common phases of matter.
Explain the physical characteristics of solids, liquids, and gases.
Describe the arrangement of atoms in solids, liquids, and gases.
summary_html: • A fluid is a state of matter that yields to sideways or shearing forces. Liquids and gases are both fluids. Fluid statics is the physics of stationary fluids.

figures.original_caption: (a) Atoms in a solid always have the same neighbors, held near home by forces represented here by springs. These atoms are essentially in contact with one another. A rock is an example of a solid. This rock retains its shape because of the forces holding its atoms together. (b) Atoms in a liquid are also in close contact but can slide over one another. Forces between them strongly resist attempts to push them closer together and also hold them in close contact. Water is an example of a liquid. Water can flow, but it also remains in an open container because of the forces between its atoms. (c) Atoms in a gas are separated by distances that are considerably larger than the size of the atoms themselves, and they move about freely. A gas must be held in a closed container to prevent it from moving out freely. (d) A plasma is composed of electrons, protons, and ions that, like gases, are spaced far apart and move about freely.

exercises.prompt: What physical characteristic distinguishes a fluid from a solid?

answer.solution: A fluid yields to a shearing force, which is a force applied sideways along a surface, and so it flows, whereas a solid resists a shearing force and keeps its shape. Note that resistance to compression does not tell the two apart, because liquids resist compression nearly as well as solids do; it is the response to shear that makes the distinction. On the atomic level, the atoms of a solid are held near fixed positions by forces that act like springs and cannot change neighbors, while the atoms or molecules of a fluid are free to slide past one another and change neighbors.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following substances are fluids at room temperature: air, mercury, water, glass?

answer.solution: Air, mercury, and water are fluids at room temperature. Air is a gas, and mercury and water are liquids; each of them flows, takes the shape of whatever holds it, and yields to a shearing force. Mercury is a metal, but being a metal does not make a substance a solid; what matters is whether its atoms can slide past one another, and at room temperature the atoms of mercury can. Glass is a solid at room temperature. It keeps its shape and resists shearing forces, and its atoms stay with the same neighbors. So three of the four are fluids, and glass is not.

exercises.prompt: Why are gases easier to compress than liquids and solids?

answer.solution: Think about the space between the particles and the forces between them. In a gas the molecules are separated by distances that are large compared with the size of the molecules themselves, so most of the volume of a gas is empty space, and the forces between the molecules are very weak except during a collision. Pushing the molecules closer together therefore meets little resistance, and the volume of a gas can be reduced a great deal. In a liquid or a solid the atoms are already in close contact. Pushing them closer would force the atoms into one another, and the forces between them strongly resist that, so liquids and solids change their volume very little under compression.

exercises.prompt: How do gases differ from liquids?

answer.solution: Begin with what they share: both are fluids, so both flow, yield to shearing forces, and take the shape of their container. They differ in volume and in compressibility. A liquid has a definite volume, forms a surface, stays in an open container, and resists compression, because its molecules are in close contact and held together by their mutual attraction even as they slide past one another. A gas has no definite volume; its molecules move to fill whatever container holds them, escape from an open one, and are easily pushed closer together, because the molecules are far apart with much space and little force between them. The major distinction, as the text puts it, is that gases are easily compressed whereas liquids are not.
